implementerProof.whatTheProofDidNotCover: The proof boundary for the evictor's error paths is unchanged from rounds 9 and 10 and has not widened: the arming, the backoff and the in-flight branch are each pinned at their own seam in the docs package with a control I drove, and none is reachable from outside the process, because an induction from outside also forces the listener's redial, whose sweep reaches the same outcome by another path. proof.criterion: The architect's addition: a row discriminating the ping guard from the wake cap, which the implementer's row locks as a pair. Built and driven; not landed, because the two are not separable and the measurement says so.
proof.surface: The same package and probe: ListenIdle 300 ms, NextWake 80 ms, an OnWake that sleeps 400 ms so the ping falls due while the callback is still running — the shape in which the cap, which can only shorten a wait before OnWake runs, cannot help.
proof.command: cd packages/envoy && . /legion/harness/env.sh && go test -count=3 -timeout 900s -v -run TestAListenerWhoseWakeOverrunsThePingStillPingsOnThatRound ./internal/dispatch/pglisten/   (the row, held in the working copy and then dropped)
proof.observed: The row is green at this head — the ping landed 491.9 ms, 487.2 ms and 482.6 ms after the LISTEN across three runs. On a scratch clone with the ping decision reverted to what ended the last wait (`if waking { continue }` in place of `if time.Since(proven) < l.idle()`), the row is green too, at 493.2 ms, 484.9 ms and 482.7 ms: indistinguishable. The reason is structural rather than a weakness of the row — waitFor's own cap is computed from that same stamp (`untilPing := idle - time.Since(proven)`), so there is no build in which the cap exists and the stamp does not, and the only separable choice is the ping decision itself, which is worth one loop iteration: the round after a wake-ended one is capped to about zero and pings there. I dropped the row rather than land it, because a row that cannot fail where the existing one passes is suite cost without coverage, and one described as discriminating when it does not is the vacuous-evidence trap this issue has already met twice.
proof.negativeControl: The reverted-guard clone above is the control, and its result is the finding: 493/485/483 ms against 492/487/483 ms. The architect's fallback stands — the limit is stated in the pull request body — with this measurement as the reason, and the stronger statement available now is that the limit is not a gap in testing but a property of the design: the stamp is the cap's input, so the halves cannot be present independently.

notes: The discriminating row the architect asked for is a negative result, reported as one: the ping guard and the wake cap cannot be told apart by behaviour, because waitFor's cap is computed from the guard's own stamp. The limit stated in the pull request body is therefore not a gap a future round could close with a better row; it is a property of the design. I would rather that sentence than a green row implying a discrimination it does not make.
